subject: Cognitive Science
title: Synaptic Pruning
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Synaptic Pruning.

hook.text: A toddler's brain has twice as many connections as an adult's. Growing up means losing synapses.

buildup.text: Synaptic pruning eliminates weak connections. It peaks in adolescence, following "use it or lose it."

discovery.text: Surviving connections get myelinated—wrapped in insulation that speeds signals up to 100 times.

twist.text: Pruning moves from back to front. The prefrontal cortex—impulse control—is literally last to finish.

climax.text: This explains impulsive teens: emotional circuits are mature while the braking system is still building.

quiz.question: What does synaptic pruning do?
options: Removes weak neural connections to improve efficiency

details.summary: The brain overproduces synaptic connections in early childhood, then prunes unused ones during adolescence and early adulthood. This use-it-or-lose-it process refines neural circuits based on experience. Pruning makes the brain more efficient by eliminating unnecessary connections.
details.whyItMatters: Synaptic pruning explains why early experience shapes the brain so powerfully. Connections that are exercised survive; those that are not are eliminated.
takeaways: The brain overproduces synapses in early development
Unused connections are pruned during adolescence
Pruning makes neural circuits more efficient and specialized

faq.question: When does synaptic pruning happen?
faq.answer: Synaptic density peaks around age two for sensory areas and later for prefrontal regions. Pruning then continues through adolescence and into the early twenties. Different brain regions prune on different timelines, with higher-order areas pruning last.

faq.question: Is synaptic pruning related to mental illness?
faq.answer: Possibly. Excessive pruning during adolescence has been linked to schizophrenia, where too many connections may be eliminated. Insufficient pruning has been associated with autism. Research is ongoing, but abnormal pruning appears to play a role in several neurodevelopmental conditions.
